title: Bo: come, not go (Exodus 10:1)
hook: God tells Moses "come unto Pharaoh", as if God is already in the room
tomorrow: Bo: darkness that could be felt (Exodus 10:21–23)

segments.voice: Yesterday, parashah, the weekly portion. Your line was the scroll keeps rolling. Today it rolls into a new portion, and its very first word.

There's a difference between a coach who says go out there and one who says come on, out we go. Same field, same game. But one of them is staying on the bench, and the other is walking out beside you. Moses has stood before Pharaoh again and again. Plague after plague, and each time Pharaoh ends up saying no. Moses has every reason to dread going back. And the portion opens with God sending him back, using a word that, in Hebrew, is a little strange. It isn't the word for go. It's the word for come.
screen: `GO OUT THERE, OR COME ON.` → `PLAGUE AFTER PLAGUE, STILL NO.` → `NOT GO. COME.`

segments.voice: The portion is named for that word: Bo. In Hebrew, God says to Moses, bo el Par'oh. The old Jewish translation, like the King James, smooths it into go in unto Pharaoh, and that's fair: the Hebrew verb can mean entering. But its plain sense is come. And people who say come are usually already where they're asking you to be. The Zohar, a classic work of Jewish mysticism, plays with exactly this. It pictures God leading Moses inward, room after room, into the innermost chamber of Pharaoh's power, the place Moses most feared, and saying: come. Not go there alone. Come here, where I already am. It's a reading, not the plain story, and the Zohar wraps it in a lot of symbolism about the deep places of evil. The simple point doesn't need the symbolism. Back at the burning bush, Moses had asked who he was to stand before Pharaoh. God's answer was a short promise: "Certainly I will be with thee." Bo is that promise, folded into one syllable. It doesn't make the room less hard. The verse even says, right there, that Pharaoh's heart has been hardened. He'll still say no. Moses still has to walk in. He just doesn't walk in first.
screen: `BO EL PAR'OH: COME UNTO PHARAOH.` · `COME: SOMEONE IS ALREADY THERE.` · `THE ZOHAR: ROOM AFTER ROOM.` · `I WILL BE WITH THEE.` · then, large: `COME, NOT GO.`

segments.voice: Think of a room you're dreading this week, a meeting, a phone call, a doctor's office, a kitchen where an old argument lives, and picture walking through its door, not as the first one in, but as someone called in by a voice already inside. If you pray, hold the words I will be with thee as you cross the threshold; if not, picture one person who'd be on your side in there.
Bo. Come. The name of this week's portion, and the word God uses to send Moses back to Pharaoh, as if calling him into a room God is already in.
Your line: come, not go. The room stays hard, but you don't walk in first. Day three hundred thirty-three, done.

howItsDone: Bo is read in synagogues in winter. Some teachers, Hasidic commentators among them, dwell on its first word, reading 'come' as a sign that God goes ahead of Moses into Pharaoh's palace.

chat.meaning: The plain sense of bo is come, and whoever says come is already there, like the promise: I will be with thee.
